citation: The impact of persistent precarity on patients' capacity to manage their treatment burden: a qualitative study of people with HIV and multimorbidity in urban and rural South Africa (2023). Frontiers in Medicine 10:1061190. doi:10.3389/fmed.2023.1061190

claims.text: Persistent income precarity makes treatment and healthy-living demands read as financially impossible, so care is delayed, traded off, or paid for with borrowed money, and anything requiring out-of-pocket spending or nutritious food is judged out of reach.
evaluative_rules: Judge a treatment or healthy-living demand by whether it can be afforded without borrowing or sacrificing other essentials
objections: Will this require money I do not have, or food I cannot afford?
vocabulary: take each day as it comes

readings.text: Someone who borrows money just to get to the clinic would weigh any new product or service by whether it removes the need for travel or can be reached without spending money they do not have.

If a person is already buying boosters and vitamins one at a time, they would assess a new product or service by whether it can be bought in small, separate amounts rather than as a single larger outlay.

Someone who feels doctors ignore that there is nothing in their rural area would be more open to a new product or service only if it does not depend on nutritious food being available or affordable where they live.

If a person is selling sheep heads to add to an old age grant because they want fresh foods, they would judge a new product or service by whether it helps them get those foods without requiring another difficult trade-off.

claims.text: Dependence on others for treatment costs turns asking for help into a source of guilt and shame, so patients keep seeking care while carrying debt or go without medication when support runs out, and anything assuming reliable family or financial backing is read as unrealistic.
evaluative_rules: Judge a treatment option by whether it can be sustained without burdening or shaming the people who help you
objections: Will this force me to keep asking others for money I cannot repay?

readings.text: Someone who keeps seeking care while carrying debt would weigh a new service by whether it reduces the need to ask others for help, since asking is a source of guilt and shame.
If a person goes without medication when support runs out, they would see a new service as unrealistic if it assumes reliable family backing.

Someone who feels constantly guilty about incurring expenses for treatment would be open to a new service that lessens dependence on others, but only if it does not add to the debt they already carry.
If a person keeps seeking care while carrying debt, they would read any new service that assumes reliable financial backing as out of touch with their situation.

claims.text: Unsafe or inaccessible home terrain makes moving about and travelling alone read as risky and physically hard, so patients wait for companions, take dangerous routes, or struggle with mobility aids, and anything requiring frequent clinic travel or home mobility is judged unsafe or impractical.
evaluative_rules: Judge a treatment or service by whether it can be reached and used without unsafe travel or difficult movement
objections: Will I have to travel alone or move around in ways that are unsafe or too hard for me?

readings.text: Someone who says moving about in the shack with a wheelchair became too hard would weigh any new service that still requires moving about at home as impractical.
If a person says it is not safe to stay where they are, they would judge a new service that depends on home visits or home mobility as unsafe.
Someone who waits for a companion to walk with from the clinic would see a new service that requires frequent clinic travel alone as risky.

If a person says they will just take the chance and go into the forest alone when companions take too long, they would weigh a new service that reduces the need for that route as safer, but would still see any required solo travel as a huge risk.

claims.text: Household violence and substance-use stress are read as direct causes of worsening illness, so patients accept their conditions and treat adherence to clinic guidance as the best available response, and home monitoring or self-management is judged helpful mainly when it reduces clinic dependence.
evaluative_rules: Judge a new health tool by whether it reduces the burden of getting to and depending on the clinic
objections: Will this actually reduce my dependence on clinic visits, or just add another thing to manage?

readings.text: Someone who has accepted their conditions and treats adherence to clinic guidance as the best available response would judge a new home monitoring tool mainly by whether it reduces clinic dependence.

If a person sees household violence and substance-use stress as direct causes of worsening illness, they may be less open to a new self-management approach that asks them to take on more responsibility at home.

Someone who believes the best they can do is adhere to nurse guidance and not miss clinic dates would weigh a new product or policy by whether it fits within that clinic-centred routine rather than replacing it.

claims.text: Health information arrives verbally from nurses and community health workers with no take-home written material, so retained information is limited and patients depend on in-person visits, making anything that assumes patients can read and follow written instructions at home a mismatch with current support.
evaluative_rules: Judge a health product or policy by whether it matches how information actually reaches and stays with patients
objections: Will I be expected to read and follow written instructions at home on my own?

readings.text: Someone who relies on nurses and community health workers to share information verbally would weigh a new product or service by whether it can be explained in person during a visit, since no papers are given to take home.

If health information is only shared verbally and no papers are given to take home, a new product or service that assumes written instructions can be followed at home would be seen as a mismatch with current support.

Someone who depends on in-person visits from nurses and community health workers to check on them and share information would be more open to a new product or service that fits into those visits rather than one that expects independent use at home.

If retained information is limited because nothing is given to take home, a new product or service that includes a way for nurses or community health workers to repeat or reinforce information during visits would be weighed more favourably than one that relies on written material.

region: Cape Town (Western Cape) and Bulungula (Eastern Cape), South Africa
confidence: One qualitative South African study: semi-structured interviews with 30 patients with HIV and other chronic conditions at public clinics in urban Cape Town and rural Eastern Cape, 2021. Mechanisms durable; the sample is people with HIV, so HIV-specific detail does not carry to every chronic illness.
subject: the money and travel a long-term illness costs every month to keep getting care
